content: A morula, derived from the Latin word morus meaning mulberry, represents an early stage of embryonic development. At this stage, the embryo consists of approximately 12 to 32 cells, known as blastomeres, which are arranged in a solid spherical structure enclosed within the zona pellucida. The morula is formed through a process called embryonic cleavage, which involves the rapid division of the zygote. Once the morula reaches the 16-cell stage, the blastomeres begin to differentiate. The inner blastomeres will eventually develop into the inner cell mass, while the outer blastomeres on the surface will flatten and form the trophoblast, which contributes to the placenta. During this differentiation process, the blastomeres undergo a morphological transformation, changing their shape and aligning tightly with one another to create a compact ball of cells. This phenomenon is referred to as compaction and is believed to be facilitated by cell surface adhesion glycoproteins. In mammals, the morula migrates to the uterus approximately 3 to 4 days after fertilization. Around the fourth day post-fertilization, a fluid-filled cavity known as the blastocoel forms within the morula. This marks the transition of the morula into the blastocyst stage, a critical step in early embryonic development.
